title: Postcards and Weather
premise: Rosalind Coldharbour, once the conservatory's most celebrated prodigy before a public collapse he refuses to explain, returns seven years later as a janitor, hiding in plain sight among the practice rooms he used to own. There he is found by Ansel Vey, the last speaker of a dying language, who demands Rosalind become his final student—an apprenticeship that forces him back into music, memory, and the orbit of his estranged family, all of whom arranged their lives around the question he has never answered: what really happened the night he walked away. As Ansel's health fails and Rosalind's sister Marguerite arrives to broker a family reconciliation built on silence, he must choose between the justice his family demands and the truth that would free him. In the end, Rosalind performs Ansel's transcribed songs at the old man's funeral—openly, under his own name—and asks the question at last, receiving an answer that costs him the family but returns him to himself.
about_author: Wren Ravensworth is the pen name of a former conservatory librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's manuscripts before writing about the ones that got away. Postcards and Weather is the second novel, written in the margins of night shifts and dedicated to the last speakers of small things.

chapters.title: The Man Who Mops in E Minor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He cleans the conservatory at night, memorizing the building's acoustics, dodging former colleagues who half-recognize him. A postcard from his mother arrives, unopened for months, weather-stained in his locker. Emotional beat: the exquisite control of a life built on almosts, and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: Ansel Vey, Age Unknown
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He finds an old man sleeping in the rehearsal annex, humming a melody in no scale Rosalind knows. Ansel addresses him by his childhood nickname—proof someone has been watching. Emotional beat: the vertigo of being seen after seven years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: A Language of Eleven Speakers, Then Ten
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel recounts the death of the tenth speaker and his own diagnosis, delivered in the flat tone of a weather report. He explains why he chose Rosalind: a prodigy who threw away his gift is the only one who might understand what a language is for. Emotional beat: grief worn as practicality.

chapters.title: Lessons Begin at 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Secret dawn lessons in the annex: Ansel teaches sounds with no notation, words for kinds of rain Rosalind's language lacks. The janitor's schedule becomes a disguise for devotion. Emotional beat: the dangerous joy of being good at something again.

chapters.title: Marguerite Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Rosalind's sister arrives as the family's emissary, armed with a plan: a reconciliation dinner, a public statement, the family narrative restored. She spots her brother's mop cart outside the annex and says nothing—yet. Emotional beat: love expressed as management, duty mistaken for care.

chapters.title: The Night It Rained Applause
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, in flashback. The collapse seven years ago: the premiere, the trembling hands, the father's face in the third row, and the lie Rosalind let stand about why he stopped. Emotional beat: the reader finally sees the wound the whole family organized itself around.

chapters.title: Words for Weather That Hasn't Invented Itself Yet
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel teaches the future tense, which his language builds from weather: you do not predict, you prepare the ground. He begins recording Rosalind's voice without asking. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by the ethics of legacy—who owns what is given.

chapters.title: The Dinner of Arranged Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The family dinner proceeds like a score everyone memorized except him. His father offers a scripted absolution contingent on continued silence. Rosalind almost says it—almost—and swallows the truth whole. Emotional beat: the cost of the almost, tasted fresh.

chapters.title: Postcards, Unsent
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite finds a shoebox of Rosalind's unsent postcards, seven years of letters to the family he couldn't face, each one stopping before the confession. She reads them all in one night. Emotional beat: her loyalty to the family narrative begins to fracture.

chapters.title: The Conservatory Discovers Its Janitor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A student hears him playing the annex piano at dawn; by afternoon, a video circulates. The conservatory that once crowned him now gawks. The dean offers a 'second chance' that is really a transaction. Emotional beat: invisibility pricing itself out of reach.

chapters.title: Ansel Refuses the Hospital
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel, declining, refuses treatment to keep teaching, and makes Rosalind transcribe the songs before the words go. He reveals he has known the family's secret all along—he was the accompanist at the collapsed premiere. Emotional beat: the student realizes the teacher chose him as much for the wound as for the gift.

chapters.title: What the Father Arranged
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite confronts their father and learns the full machinery: the review he suppressed, the career he redirected, the silence he purchased. She understands the family was built around protecting his version of events. Emotional beat: justice outside the law begins to look like the only kind available.

chapters.title: The Question, Almost
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind stands outside his father's study with the postcards in his coat, rehearsing the question. A phone call about Ansel's collapse interrupts; he chooses the annex over the study. Emotional beat: the almost again—but this time it feels like a choice, not a failure.

chapters.title: Eleven Songs for a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Bedridden, Ansel dictates the final songs—each one about a different kind of leaving. He tells Rosalind a language survives only if someone is willing to be embarrassing with it. Emotional beat: mortality as deadline, and permission as inheritance.

chapters.title: Marguerite Breaks Rank
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite mails one of the unsent postcards to their father, forcing the crisis she was sent to prevent. She chooses her brother over the family's architecture of silence. Emotional beat: the emissary defects; duty and love finally point the same direction.

chapters.title: The Confrontation in the Practice Room
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Father and son meet in the annex. Rosalind asks the question the whole family arranged itself around: why did you let the lie stand? The answer—shame, dressed as protection—lands without absolution. Emotional beat: the truth spoken at last, and the discovery that it frees him and costs him everything at once.

chapters.title: Ansel's Last Weather
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel's final days: he teaches the word for 'goodbye that expects return,' makes Rosalind promise to sing the songs publicly, and dies at dawn during a rain his language has a specific name for. Emotional beat: grief and gratitude in the same breath; the last speaker becomes the first ancestor.

chapters.title: The Offer Withdrawn
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The dean offers a restored career contingent on keeping the family story intact; Rosalind refuses, quitting the janitor's job that kept him safe. His father cuts contact; Marguerite does not. Emotional beat: the prodigy chooses the small true thing over the large false one.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for the Living
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He rehearses Ansel's songs in the empty annex, voice failing, starting over, teaching two conservatory students the pronunciation so the language will outlive the funeral. Emotional beat: the almost-saying ends; he says it, out loud, to an empty room, and it holds.

chapters.title: The Funeral Performance
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs, braided. At Ansel's funeral, Rosalind performs the eleven songs under his own name, announcing the language and its new speakers. The conservatory listens; his father does not come; Marguerite sits in the front row. Emotional beat: the climax—identity claimed publicly, justice rendered without a courtroom.

chapters.title: Postcard, Sent
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. He mails his father one final postcard containing the truth, with no demand for reply, and begins teaching a small evening class in Ansel's language. Emotional beat: release—the question answered no longer needs an audience.

chapters.title: Weather, Continuing
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, one year later. The annex class has five students; Marguerite visits; a new postcard arrives, unsigned, containing only their childhood nickname. Rosalind opens the windows and lets the rain in. Emotional beat: resolution—not restoration, but a life finally weatherproofed by truth instead of silence.
